text: July 2024 I bought my first AMD GPU in many years (10+) after having nothing but problems with the FirePro Workstation GPUs and losing $1000s of dollars on them.  I bought an AMD ASUS TUF Gaming Radeon RX 7800 XT 16GB unit.  It replaced an ASUS TUF Gaming RTX-3080 10GB in my R9-5950X 128GB system.  The 7800 XT traded blows with my RTX-3080 on most tests that I made.  The main reason why I bought it though was for testing my software on team red (I am a 3D software developer).  Unfortunately the OpenGL performance on large triangle count scenes is really bad on the AMD.  My software will render up to 135 million triangle scenes, and the 7800 XT drops to a measly 12 fps.  Even my old RTX-2060 6GB beats it for fps in this scene test.  But overall I am pleased with the AMD GPU.  It was plug and play for the most part, although the driver took way longer than team green to install.  Next I need to get an Intel Battlemage for a test system for my software.  Assuming Intel doesn't drop out of the GPU race, their CPU woes at this time and low GPU sales may make for some fun times for Intel.

text:
The thing is, most "serious" PC gamers will still only be on a budget of $2500/£2000ish for their rig, that means realistically they'll be running a 1080p or 1440p 144hz monitor, a 6/12 or 8/16 CPU that isn't flagship, Ram with decent CAS latency but not ultra low latency, and will be left with maybe 600-900ish for their GPU. Outside of that price rage the budget builders on sub $2000 budgets will outnumber the big budget enthusiasts at least 5 to 1, if not more much more.
The state of the economy means this is unlikely to change during this generation of GPUs (next 2 years of so). This is something Game devs will be aware of and they'll target the largest portion of the market to maximise accessibility to their games, so if you're already packing a 3080 or like myself a 6800xt, i honestly can't see a reason to upgrade this generation unless you're looking at also upgrading to 4k or your rig is now 2 or 3 generations behind and relying on DLSS/FSR to keep your frame rate up.
My 6800xt is still beautiful, turn ray tracing off, i still feel like it's overrated/underutilised anyway, and the non RT fall-back alternative you're left with still looks visually incredible anyway. But yeah, i get ultra settings with avg 90fps+ @1440p without FSR... for me, that's some serious wiggle room, i'm nowhere near the point of using FSR to maintain my FPS even on 2022 releases. And even an older gen rtx2000/amd5000 series card can max out your 144fps monitors for amateur Esport gamers who whack all their settings down to low anyway.

text:
I got the XFX Merc Black rx6750xt brand new in early June2022 for 599€ cause i was tired of my gtx970 performance, i also needed to complete my 2021's r7-5800x new build. The old launch drivers of this card were good and the performance was already close to a 3070 and was boosting at ~2750mhz. With the latest drivers the stuttering it's gone, s.a.m. it's giving me even more fps than before. I then decided to do a small undervolt 1152mV, and find a global stable oc... I'm at 2823mhz on core,  2312mhz + fast timings on vRAM, +4% Power Limit (from 230w to 240w tdp). Now i match a 3070ti with fps in 1440p@144hz gaming, but i'm in the overclocked 3070 territory on benchmarks. I can go higher (2900+MHz / +15%PL) but i need to waterblock the card cause i don't like see the hotspot at 109°C instead of 99°C in the worst case scenarios... 

Two years ago i wanted an rtx3070/rtx2080ti so badly, but now i have a more powerful red card! I always play in raster3D cause RT it's not adding anything to the gameplay yet, and i've yet to try FSR2: my mates with 3070s have to use dlss to match my card's performance without FSR on 🤣

text:
As an RTX 3080 owner, I've got to say that ray tracing is overrated. DLSS is also not that big of a deal when FSR works as well as it does. Ultimately, using no upscaling at all is still better, which is another reason why DLSS isn't important to have. Standard rasterized performance per dollar is more important!

Ray tracing is still ultimately not that practical, because there are more efficient ways of getting better image quality. Ray tracing just costs too much performance to be worth using, except when you have so much performance to spare that it doesn't matter. Ray tracing is always going to be the first thing that you want to turn off in order to improve fps. In other words, ray tracing as a feature doesn't end up mattering much in the long run, but it is nice to have if you're talking about the absolute most expensive graphics card.

And, for the record, I'm a big Cyberpunk and Control fan, which is why I ever even considered getting an RTX 3080, but I was a bit disappointed with how subtle the ray tracing actually is. The lighting still looks amazing in both games even WITHOUT ray tracing, and the fps is WAY WAY higher. Cyberpunk also still requires DLSS at 1440p with ray tracing on a 3080, and I'm really not sold on DLSS in Cyberpunk (I was previously using FSR with an overclocked 1070 ti in cyberpunk at 1440p, and was very happy with how much of an improvement it gave over running at 1080p). At least I still got a good enough used price on a good quality 3080, which still has over a year of manufacturer warranty coverage from EVGA, that I don't really mind that the ray-tracing has been disappointing.

author: @Nerex7

text:
@Nerex7  The 7900xtx has equal price to performance in RT as a 4080. That was AMDs stated goal and they reached that stated goal. 

It’s 20% slower and 20% cheaper. That’s great! Every other gpu in this generation gets worse price to performance as it gets cheaper. 

There is no reason to cover for AMD where they do not even need cover. This is a halo product and should be compared on the halo settings of a game. If Raster was all that matters, then AMD would price it equal to the 4080 as it can beat the 4080 in raster. Instead AMD priced the gpu at the price to performance equivalent of RT. 

We are not comparing $500 mid range gpus, where you may turn down settings to high or medium for better fps. These are the best of the best and should be compared at the highest settings, full stop.  

If you just want a good gaming experience, but not necessarily the best graphical settings. Then just buy a ps5 or last gen AMD card, they will do an amazing job for around half the price. 


For a metaphor: a Dodge Challenger and Ford Mustang could have the same HP, but a single spec doesn’t not make the entire car. Torque, traction, turning radius, handling, etc all play a roll as well and should be factored into the review/purchase.

text:
At $619 the 6900XT makes a lot of sense compared to the 6950 at $784. That's a huge bang for buck difference.

I probably should have bought the 6900XT rather than the 3080. But there's always NVIDIA fanboys willing to pay extra for them on the used market, and there are a few useful features that the 6000 series didn't have so I bought a 3080 for a couple hundred less without any shame.


As for the 7900XTX versus 4080. Right now, mostly that's above performance parity for a 20% better price (with a few just below performance parity exceptions), and at best about 15-20% better for 20% less coin.

Looking back at the 6900XT versus the 7900XTX. At 4k, that 53% difference roughly matches the $619 versus $999 price.
As such, for me the 6900XT if at that price is STILL a great deal. 

But if the best you can get for a 6900XT is $699, then the new cards are the winner, even without future driver improvements.

Don't buy on a promise. Buy the product you can get.

If you mainly game on Japanese developed games, their approach to ray tracing is actually quite reserved with only Capcom's RE Engine being the one which is more willing to give ray tracing support. (And to their credit, their implimentation works surprisingly well even on a Radeon card.)
But depending on the title, even if the RE engine supports ray tracing, Capcom will adjust whether or not they'll put raytracing into a game. Like Monster Hunter Rise: Sunbreak is one of those games that is based on RE Engine but don't have ray tracing support.
All in all, for those who focus on Japanese or indie games, you're really just paying for a feature that you won't come by so often in the first place, since most Japanese developers still lean more on raw raster then ray tracing.

For Gamers that stick with Nvidia: Stop sweating over Ray Tracing. 

If you want to play your games at 4K (well, 3.8K) ultra/maxxed presets at 120fps with ray tracing on, then come back maybe two or 3 cards from now, and maybe ray tracing won't be so much of a gimmick by then. Try the RTX 6090 LOL

I kept my 1080ti while everyone else seemed to be sprinting out to grab up 2xxx-series cards. It was so funny. I absolutely skipped the 2080ti. I of course bought two RTX Titans (since i always collected them), and even with the RTX Titans, ray tracing was a gimmick. If you can't help yourself with ray tracing, and just HAVE TO have it, then don't buy anything less than the top end card.

text: ​ @freaky425  It might seem that this is AMD problem at first but actually it is the monitor manufacturer to blame as @hyperevade wrote. You need to understand how the driver is switching the states in order to lower/increase core and memory freq. The switching needs to be done in the blanking space after the GPU is done displaying a frame on the monitor otherwise you would experience blinking so that's why it stays at max freq when there is really small time window in which the freq could be changed as the freq switch also takes some time in microseconds. The timings are stored in the monitor by manufacturer and read by the GPU and this is different for each resolution and refresh rate but can be overridden manually by the user.

text:
@antonliakhovitch8306  I was being conservative as the person i was replying to, if i'm remembering correctly, had made many anti-AMD comments.
Also:
- while ray tracing isnt super important today, it will likely become more important for many users since it might become an omnipresent feature.
- DLSS is still a feature AMD has no awnser for (FSR 2.0 is cool but its not as good or the same). Its not essential but many games already have support for it and it's arguably free FPS.
- CUDA isn't only for AI researchers, CUDA is extremely common in numerous data processing tasks. And AI video upscaling, AI video frame interpolation and other tasks that enthusiasts can make use of are very very often drastically faster using CUDA.
All Adobe Software support AMD but there are significant advantages when using CUDA compatible GPUs in some of their tools (Premiere Pro, Photoshop, AfterEffect). Sony Vegas, MAYA, Final Cut Pro,  and more all heavily benefit from CUDA too.

All in all, AMD GPUs are making heaps of progress and, when doing only gaming, they are up to snuff in many/most scenarios, but they do have downsides which need to be mentionned.

I'm very hyped to see the state of AMD GPUs in 6 months+ and i'm glad they are now good enough that I can recommend them to my friends who are on a budget. But we shouldn't be blinded by what we want them to be, AMD still has work in front of them in key areas.

author: @resresres1

text: @anonanon7368  Agreed, but contrary to popular belief, AMD was far superior to Nvidia for compute performance not that long ago. Cryptominers used AMD exclusively for a long time for exactly this reason (and not just performance per watt). They were just faster. But using CUDA is so much easier to use, it's ridiculous. Being limited by OpenCL and Nvidia never releasing anything other than the earliest of drivers for OpenCL, library considerations and the overhead of using OpenCL, CUDA started being faster. Nvidia had their developers actually create assembly code for some of its GPU libraries. Just compare clBLAS vs cuBLAS. cuBLAS is way faster than clBLAS on the same Nvidia GPU. On AMD, it can only use clBLAS and ends up being slower. Then add in tensor cores... though AMD has added their own version, but I haven't kept up with recent changes because of prices.

text:
Not gonna lie, Linus totally made this sound like such a win for AMD lol.  I mean I even felt a bit better hearing this over every other video.  So much so I'm like well maybe I will return my 4080 for this.

But the truth is there is a LOT of under emphasized hope in optimizations and all of that (even though he said this twice).  This is a solid case of getting your newly released game that needs the DLC to become worth it.

It's absolutely frustrating that at this price point a lot of the justification is on "potential" and speculation of better drivers.  

The truth is if you buy a 7900 XTX the questions are. . Are you fine with turning ray tracing completely off for every game that ever comes out in the future?  Are you ok with giving up DLSS Quality's superior picture quality and performance (some games this can be significant where others barely look different)? Are you ok if performance never actually changes from its current state on the XTX? Are you ok with the higher temps and power draw quarks the 7900 card has?  Is spending an extra $200 negligible for the 4080?

To me it's very tough because AMD's pricing on this sucks.  Over hyped and Over priced.  Like Nvidia, they are not innocent here.
Another potential issue is, what happens when AIB cards with good coolers cost $1,200.  We'll see tomorrow but I am not optimistic.

Efficiency while gaming is nuts and the card runs stable at a slight undervolt (-70mV).

I am not entirely happy switching from Nvidia to AMD. Given similar performance, efficiency and price I'd go Nvidia again. Those early crashes and blue screen woes have soured my experience.

-RTX 3050: ~3500 points

-RTX3060: ~4800 points

So no, no lies. The difference is that RDNA2 shares RT performance with rasterized performance, if you use "Ultra" + RT they fare worse, but once you dial in optimized settings, the RT performance is much better than benchmarks make them out to seem.

text:
Linus (& Co), to make things easier to see for us semi-colorblind folks, can you group together some parts of your graphs (specifically thermal/power consumption)? For example: 4090 and 4080 could use triangles in place of dots and there could be two colors (one bright and one dark) to differentiate the way they look. Then 6xxx could use squares and 7xxx could use dots. This would especially be helpful against a red background considering 8% of males have an issue with colorblindness and 95%+ of those people have an issue with red/green. If you assume that 90% of your viewers are male and 8% of males have a form of colorblindness and 95% of those are red/green, then you can assume 6.8% of your audience would have some form of an issue with these elements. Not significant, but also not insignificant.

Also, as the number of fps grows with each generation, it may be more useful to use a standard multiple of the likes used in rack setups. For example: set 60fps = 1 standard unit. Therefore, if a game only achieves 30fps, we are shown 0.5 on a graph. On the other end of the spectrum, we would see 120fps = 2 standard units and 480fps = 8 standard units. Although raw fps is useful to look at, a comparison to a standard that most gamers would agree to be standard would make it simple to say X-card does 1.5 and Y-card does 2.1; a clear winner but a much cleaner user interface. Additionally, this  works excellent at sub 60fps. If a game with RT-on can only achieve 0.3 and another can achieve 0.7, then you can quickly do math in your head to say that 0.7 is over double 0.3 (exactly 2.3x), whereas 18fps and 42fps are a bit more cumbersome. I know it would be difficult to move the industry to adopt this naming scheme but it may put pressure on GPU manufacturers to maintain a 60fps minimum so they aren't labelled with the "sub-standard" name brand moniker.

Thanks for listening. I enjoy (most of :P) your videos. Keep it up!

text:
When it comes to raytracing I think we're seeing the results of Nvidia's "throw the kitchen sink at it" approach to making an absolute beefhouse of a card. The horsepower is spread out between those RT cores and the main graphics pieces, which shows when the RT isn't being pushed to its limits. If you're not hitting both, then your RTX 4000 series won't show its Final Form.

Maybe there isn't space for it in the review, but I think it's deserving of a deep-dive to test out specifically RT games on Nvidia and AMD, and run them at different RT performance and DLSS-equivalent settings, to see if those more moderate settings make an impact on the value comparison. Would also be useful to dig into whether those more moderate settings are noticeably worse, and highlight how it changes the look of the RT effects. Right now, you make it sound like raytracing is an on/off switch, and putting it on instantly makes Nvidia the clear winner, but to my mind it's just another setting in the menu. When you turn something up to max and it tanks your performance, you naturally should look for a more reasonable level to leave it on. To me, the review process of capping out every setting makes sense for comparison's sake, but it very much doesn't tell the whole picture, especially now that we're dealing with a specific setting that's a headlining feature of certain graphics cards.

text:
I am middle aged so I've had several Nvidia, AMD and ATI before they were bought by AMD, video cards, as well as others before them (Voodoo etc).

Recently I had AMD RX 580 that I bought from a miner in the crash of 2019 for $90. I know right, mining crashes, we've already had 2 in 3 years. Anyway that card is still working great, I gave it away even though it was worth $250 at the time about a year ago.

Currently I have NVIDIA RTX 1080 Ti 11GB and it plays games well. I'm only on 1080p, but according to Steam's Hardware Monitor so are most of you :-)

I haven't had any problems with the AMD or Nvidia cards or their drivers for several years.
There is a driver remover application you can download to run on Windows If you have a driver that stuck.

I always uninstall the driver before I remove the card. Then I power off the machine. Then remove the card, the driver had just been removed before I powered off.
Put in the the next card, switch on, install that driver.

I find that uninstalling the driver before removing the hardware makes everything smooth.

text: @MrGamelover23  honestly a bunch of other people in this thread had great advice. Make sure you ddu before installing your new card, be prepared for adrenaline to need to be uninstalled and reinstalled, and look at some reviews of the products you buy. I had a weird issue where my card on stock settings needed a higher power target set to avoid issues in gpu bound situations. A reviewer found the issue and I had no issues once I discovered that was my issue. A friend also bought the same card and didn't have this issue though so it's totally a card to card issue. I also found that overclocking was very different on amd vs Nvidia. On my 1070 I could basically drag all the sliders to max and enjoy the extra performance. Or I could easily Google the expected frequency for the card and plug in the numbers and be golden. My experience with rdna was not that, it required me to actually test things and was way more tuned to my card, again me and a friend bought the same card, mine wants more power target but can achieve better overclocks at the same voltage. I would also say that undervolting on my 6900xt was an experience, I was able to achieve a pretty healthy underclock but lost about 5% performance vs stock and the benefits are definitely there but I had to mess with the voltage curve a lot to get it stable. Overall I would say amd just requires a little more work to achieve what you can on Nvidia, but if you have a weekend to learn and burn you can get amazing results.

text: The one thing that keeps me going team red for my GPU is their pricing. Maybe raytracing is worth several hundred dollars more on the hardware, to the right user, but as far as I can tell it’s solely a gimmick to try and fleece you, and AMD performs just as well for what I care about for cheaper.
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: Ray tracing definitely isn’t a gimmick, but it’s also not worth paying so much more to have.
author: @lamsmiley1944

text: @lamsmiley1944  But it kinda sorta is a gimmick. It attracts your attention, and because of that you pay money for it, and that’s literally all that’s required for it to be just a gimmick. There’s not a real tangible benefit to most consumers who shell out for it.
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: @cheeseisgreat24  there’s real and tangible advantages to moving to ray traced lighting. Not only does it improve visuals, it has the potential to significantly reduce production time. It’ll be the standard in the next few years, gimmicks are popular for a short period then fade into obscurity.
author: @lamsmiley1944

text: @lamsmiley1944  Enhancing visuals for people who have cards capable of running it. If you don’t it doesn’t improve visuals at all. So having it be industry standard would be a weird decision since you’re cutting your game’s visual legs off for a huge portion of the market.
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: @cheeseisgreat24  that’s how progress works. It starts with high end products and then becomes more affordable. At some point you have to stop developing for old hardware
author: @lamsmiley1944

text: @lamsmiley1944  Yea, but that’s assuming ray tracing will offer an advantage over conventional rendering. Right now it doesn’t except as a gimmick. Couple that with Nvidia demanding people have deep pockets if they want it, and the market penetration of the tech is very limited even though the tech is incredibly old and therefore should be *cheaper* instead of more expensive.
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: @cheeseisgreat24  can you explain how better graphics are a gimmick? Developers aren’t going to suddenly decide that they don’t want their games to look better
author: @lamsmiley1944

text: @lamsmiley1944 They might want it but they also have to develop for the consumer who’s gonna buy it. Any time you spend developing for the 1-10% of your consumer base that can afford beefy enough hardware to run your graphics at full res is time ultimately wasted, it doesn’t really make you any more money than if you didn’t do that. The much more likely big ticket feature of the future is AI upscaling that allows cheaper cards to perform at better resolutions than expensive ones, since ray tracing is a massive performance hit just for a few reflections and sparsely lit scenes to look nicer. 🤷🏻‍♂️
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: @lamsmiley1944  Just because *you* are enthusiastic for a feature and like to pick out the moments it makes things look nicer doesn’t mean it’s a big draw for the average consumer who doesn’t know shit about these features, and it is the average consumer that makes these companies their money, not the enthusiasts.
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: @cheeseisgreat24  All advancements start with premium pricing, but as the tech matures the price drops. Also as of 2021 nearly 20% of users had RTX cards that would have only grown over the last year. Technology isn’t stagnant and developers will continue to take advantage of new tech which in turn drives more consumers to upgrade
author: @lamsmiley1944

text: @lamsmiley1944  that’s true. But gimmicks also start at the premium price point and die out when they realize no one cares about them.
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: @lamsmiley1944  So which is more likely from a business perspective, a graphics feature most people can’t even notice whether it’s on or off will become the dominant way to sink money in to develop for and do things with, or a feature that most people will be able to detect whether it’s on or off and when it’s off they dislike the experience will become the more dominant feature to optimize for?
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: @lamsmiley1944  Just sayin’, if I’m running a company and I only have a finite number of developers and a limited budget, I know which thing I’m tasking them to optimize for, and it’s probably not the thing nobody’s gonna notice whether we do it well or not. 🤷🏻‍♂️
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: @cheeseisgreat24  if you were running a studio I’d hope that you’d understand that ray tracing saves your developers significant amounts of time as they wouldn’t have to bake the lighting every time they made a change. Time is money and using baked lighting takes far longer.
author: @lamsmiley1944

text: @lamsmiley1944  Yea, but it requires the majority of purchasers of the game to have a card capable of running it. So it doesn’t save me any time when I have to do two different renderings. 🤷🏻‍♂️
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: @cheeseisgreat24  This conversation is just going in circles. If you were developing a game you would take into account the hardware that the majority of people would have at the end of the development cycle. As it takes several years to produce a game if you started development now by the time the game was finished the majority of users would have a ray tracing capable card.
author: @lamsmiley1944

text: @lamsmiley1944  Considering that hardware accelerated ray tracing for gaming has been around for 4 years and a majority of people don’t have cards capable of running it, nor is that likely to happen in the next 4? Yeaaaaaaaaaaa no there bud. There’s a reason why still only the AAA-iest of AAA titles even bother at this point, and it’s solely for bragging rights.
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: @lamsmiley1944  By the time the majority have them, other technologies will supplant the business case for even including the feature.
author: @cheeseisgreat24

text: @cheeseisgreat24  Maybe go read about the benefits of ray tracing. You seem extremely passionate about not liking it

text:
Really sad they didn't bother mentioning Radeon Chill. Anyone who's worried about power draw (or heat output) should reallllly look into AMD's "Chill" feature. It's part of the Radeon driver software, and dynamically adjusts your FPS, depending on user input. What does that mean?

So, you can adjust the minimum FPS a game is allowed to play at, down to 30fps. Or set it to 60fps if you like. Whichever. Now, if you're in game and you step away from your PC, your frames drop down to 30FPS (or 60, or whatever you set it to.)
But as soon as you touch your mouse or keyboard, FPS jumps up to whatever the highest it can (or you've limited it to) is.
This works as you're playing as well. So if you're just watching a cutscene, and take your hands off the KB and mouse, you drop down to 30fps. Not ideal, which is why I set my minimum to 60fps. I don't need 144fps while watching a cutscene, personally lol.

This helps at menus, any time you're reading something in-game, go AFK, or whatever the case might be. It helps save a bit of power, and for me, it noticeably reduces the amount of heat being spewed out from the GPU. (I have a 6700XT.)

text:
Alternate way to look at it is that raytracing is the line on which price/performance is roughly equal between AMD 6000-7000 series and Nvidia 3000-4000 series lineups and they just have different products along the line. If Nvidia had a $900 card (which they were going with baby4080 and seem likely to with the phoenix'd 4070ti) then it will roughly equal 7900XTX in RT performance, meanwhile if AMD adds a $1,200 card it'll probably equal 4080 in RT performance (which is also quite plausible as an upclocked + v-cached MCDs 7950XTX or something in a few months).
Looked at that way, it isn't "Nvidia for raytracing, AMD for value", it's "price and raytracing are at parity currently, AMD for the option of huge res/fps raster and Nvidia for the option of GPGPU CUDA stuff or if you want to spend >$1,000"

text:
@666Tomato666  The reality is that benching 4K is always going to be more consistent a metric for VR users anyway.

While a lot of the extra trickery VR uses can be useful, it causes a lot of inconsistency with testing (and also requires the headset to be worn which functionally changes the benchmark in a lot of ways, even more so with the trickery). Ultimately the headset in VR renders two HD screens, so at best a good "VR Benchmark" is to just render a scene in stereoscopic 3D, which is not the same but not all that different from just running the 4k and 1440p benchmarks and letting VR users that have a good grasp of what that translates to in VR work with it. Fact is most VR games are meant to run on relatively equivalent hardware, so if you can run one VR game you can run most of them.

text:
Here's a note from personal experience on a 5700XT and Pixio PX275H 1440p monitor: AMD's power consumption at idle may be explained by the monitor's vblank time.

Since this is a remnant from the CRT era, LCD monitor manufacturers tend to reduce the blanking time, to save on pixel clock and power on the monitor's side. However, the reduced blanking time makes it so the memory clock just stays at the maximum at all time (1750MHz on my card), increasing the memory power consumption. Using the good ol' Display Resolution Utility to set all the monitor parameters to "standard LCD" lets the memory go back to its idle state and idle power consumption.

text:
I kind of disagree with Linus' thesis that RT performance isn't important. 
If what you care about is older games that don't support RT or upscaling you don't need a current gen GPU. Because even at 4k it will be pretty hard to notice the additional performance if you have VRR on and aren't doing a side by side comparison.
You play modern games but don't care about RT, I would still urge you to turn on upscaling. Artifacts have become pretty rare and the additional antialiasing will make it look better than native 4k in most situations. And when you use upscaling without RT last gen cards will still give you good enough performance. 
I think we have to remember that the reason why we care about the performance of our hardware isn't the number we get running benchmarks but in the experience that performance unlocks. If you aren't using RT I just don't see a (gaming related) use case where the price of a current gen over a last gen card is justified. 

A little side note. I wish gaming tech journalism would focus more on the subjective experience than raw numbers. If a game looks equally good and runs subjectively equally smooth does it matter which one get's the higher number?

text:
One thing I do get frustrated with the Blender benchmarking tool is that it uses generic GPU rendering on Radeon (it does not run HIP or any AMD optimizations) yet always runs CUDA/OptiX on nvidia GPUs that support them along with other nvidia optimizations. So the benchmarking tool is heavily skewed in nvidia's favor and does not reflect the true performance you can expect from AMD GPUs in Blender rendering. 

While ultimately AMD/HIP still lag behind nvidia/CUDA/OptiX in rendering performance, this almost entirely comes down to lack of software support/investment, not due to raw hardware performance. This benchmarking tool is a prime example. 

I do wish AMD would put more efforts into helping Blender (and others) optimize for AMD GPUs. CUDA/OptiX are good but that's only because there is no appreciable competition in that space, not because they are inherently amazing or contain some magic sauce that no one else can replicate.

Alas, I know this is not where the money flows.

"fine wine" (fīn wīn) - a nickname created by fans for a unofficial technology of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD for short), which refers to this company not being able to release stable, properly optimized drivers for their GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) products in time for their launch. Then in span of multiple years AMD keeps working on these imperfect drivers, turning their GPUs into what they should have been at their release, which makes fans of this product line jokingly say that it "ages like fine wine". AMD FineWine is a meme name for a not existing technology of AMD improving their products over the years into what they should have been to begin with.

This is making me really look forward to what these cards will be like after the teething issues and what the mid-range Radeon cards are going to be like. AMD has been killing it on their value cards for a while, and it's shaping up to be no different this generation.

I definitely agree with the conclusion at the end. It sucks that AMD releases these cards with half-assed drivers, yet at the same time they're well known to take good post-launch care of their cards, so it's a resounding "meh" in that regard.

It might be interesting to some extent to look at Linux benches when Mesa mainlines 7000 series support, as definitely one of the main reasons I've always ended up on Radeon cards is their value and general usage experience on the Mesa drivers on Linux, and the Mesa drivers are known to have different performance characteristics, including stuff like outright just having better OpenGL performance to a degree that it's almost silly.(the gap has been bridged at least somewhat from what I've heard, but it's still a good example) There's also manner in which DXVK mediates shader management and the use of Proton and WINE "normalizing" the behavior of a lot of sufficiently compatible games while maintaining framerates within error of Windows or in very rare cases above, particularly in the lows. Most Windows games, of course, will take substantial 5-10% hits to the average peak FPS or worse depending on what edge cases for the game that haven't been fixed with compatibility layers yet or if the port is simply bad on a native game(many of these bad ports run better if you just run the Windows version via WINE by forcing Proton usage in Steam settings).

text:
Buyer Beware: Something not mentioned in this video is that even if your motherboard has two or more x16 pci slots, it doesn't (and often doesn't) mean that your chipset has enough pci lanes to support using this as a second gpu. ESPECIALLY if you have anything else attached to your x8, x4, or x1 slots. 

Check the chipset of your motherboard to see how many lanes your motherboard has, and then do the math to see if you have enough for your needs. Also keep in mind, that  since AMD Zen 3, AMD chips now share PCI lanes with all USB devices and any onboard network adapters (ethernet, wifi, etc). So your math might be short if you find your second GPU running in x8 mode even if its in an x16 slot.

text:
Depends on whether they are running CUDA or OptiX in these benchmarks. There's no 40 series CUDA data on Blender's OpenData site, so I cannot verify (Looking at the scaling, it seems to be OptiX*). But AMD's performance will improve somewhat with the planned inclusion of HIP-RT in the 3.5 release, taking advantage of the RDNA 2 and 3 RT cores. The actual performance improvement is unknown, as there are no public drivers nor Blender builds that include the feature. My guess is that it still won't be anywhere near 40 series though, that's just a massive gap to close.

For reference: On OpenData, a 3090 scores 6025 with OptiX - but only 3493 with CUDA.
7900XTX scores 3804 with HIP. That's just over what a 3090 does with CUDA, and AMD's cards always seem to be slower in hardware ray tracing.
*A 4090 scores 12141 with OptiX which lines up with the ~3-3,5x scaling seen in the video, that's why I'm thinking they ran the benchmarks with OptiX. Would've been good to mention in the video though.

text:
The main problem is likely that the Mesa drivers often take up to a month or two to mainline support for new cards, and the AMD-provided Linux drivers are generally worse for most things gaming if not even in some cases for productivity too while also sharing the kind of teething issues the Windows drivers have if not worse. 

I would bet that it's not that they haven't considered testing Linux, but moreso that testing Linux without reasonable driver support on representative use cases is unproductive, and that they're ending up well out of the normal hardware release cycle when or if they do so later on top of the limited benchmarking tools which are usefully representative of Linux use cases, god bless Phoronix for their test suite.

On top of that, it's important to remember the tendency for performance abnormalities to some degree. Last time I used GNOME3, for example, I had 30% worse performance in games than when I was on i3wm, and honestly I don't really know why given that both were on X11 and in theory iirc true fullscreen games were supposed to not be held back by Mutter. I didn't test on KDE, but it likely would not have had such a ridiculous gap. That was back right around 5700XT release, so I bet the results are also far better today. 

They'll have to learn an entire new set of "possible fringe reasons that framerates would vary widely", and we will have to live with, if they do decide to start picking up Linux benchmarks, that the informational value of those benchmarks could vary far more widely than their Windows benchmarks. The other thing to think about is that the relative performance metrics also apply mostly cleanly to Linux as well even though they are only looking at Windows, and, as I noted earlier, the boys at Phoronix already maintain high quality Linux benching for the most part. Maybe this is something they eventually pick up with LTT labs, but it's definitely more a curiosity than urgency if anything else.
